content: Long COVID, also referred to as Long COVID Syndrome, long-haul COVID, post-COVID-19 condition, post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC), or chronic COVID syndrome (CCS), is a condition characterized by persistent symptoms following an acute COVID-19 infection. These symptoms can involve multiple organ systems and may significantly impact daily functioning. Overview Shortly after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, studies revealed that a significant proportion of patients who recovered from acute COVID-19 continued to experience long-term symptoms. This condition has been described using various terms, including long COVID and post-COVID-19 syndrome. The lack of standardized terminology has complicated the characterization of its epidemiology, risk factors, clinical features, and treatment options. Symptoms of long COVID can manifest as a combination of respiratory, cardiovascular, neurological, urological, and gastrointestinal issues. The most commonly reported symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath (dyspnea), and cognitive dysfunction (often referred to as brain fog by patients). These symptoms may arise after the initial recovery from acute COVID-19 or persist from the acute phase. They can also fluctuate or relapse over time. Historical Perspective The term long COVID was first introduced as a hashtag on Twitter by a patient who was not recovering as expected from COVID-19. This patient-coined term quickly gained acceptance among the public and medical professionals. Since September 2020, the condition has been classified in the ICD-10 system as post-COVID-19 condition. Definition On October 6, 2021, the World Health Organization (WHO) released a clinical case definition for post-COVID-19 condition. According to the WHO, post-COVID-19 condition occurs in individuals with a history of probable or confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, typically three months from the onset of COVID-19, with symptoms lasting at least two months that cannot be explained by an alternative diagnosis. Common symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath, and cognitive dysfunction, which often interfere with daily functioning. Symptoms may be new-onset following recovery from acute COVID-19 or persist from the initial illness. They may also fluctuate or relapse over time. A separate definition may apply to children. Pathophysiology The exact mechanisms underlying long COVID are not fully understood, but several hypotheses have been proposed: 1. Long-term tissue damage: Persistent symptoms may result from damage to various organs during the acute phase of COVID-19. For example: Respiratory symptoms: Lung fibrosis may cause ongoing shortness of breath and cough. Neurological symptoms: Structural and metabolic abnormalities in the brain and brainstem may lead to symptoms such as headache, memory loss, anosmia, and fatigue. Fatigue: Chronic fatigue may arise from autonomic nervous system dysfunction, inflammation, channelopathies, or inadequate cerebral perfusion. Cardiovascular symptoms: Cardiac injury during acute COVID-19, such as myocardial inflammation or impaired contractile function, may result in chest pain, palpitations, and tachycardia. 2. Ongoing inflammation: Persistent inflammation has been observed in some patients recovering from COVID-19. This may be due to: Viral persistence: The virus may remain in the gastrointestinal tract, as evidenced by studies showing its presence in gastric and intestinal cells. Immune dysregulation: Elevated inflammatory markers (e.g., CRP, IL-6, D-dimer) and lymphopenia during acute COVID-19 have been associated with long COVID symptoms, including myalgia, fatigue, and joint pain. 3. Autoimmunity: Dysfunction of T-cells and B-cells has been suggested to contribute to long COVID pathophysiology, resembling autoimmune diseases. 4. Exercise intolerance: Studies using invasive cardiopulmonary exercise testing (iCPET) have shown that patients without underlying cardiopulmonary disease who recovered from COVID-19 exhibit reduced peak oxygen consumption, impaired systemic oxygen extraction, and abnormal ventilatory efficiency during exercise. Epidemiology and Demographics The prevalence of long COVID varies across studies due to differences in definitions and terminology. A meta-analysis involving 47,910 patients estimated that 80% of individuals with SARS-CoV-2 infections developed at least one long-term symptom lasting between 14 and 110 days. Women appear to be more commonly affected than men. Persistent symptoms reported include chest pain, breathing difficulties, muscle pain, anosmia, and fatigue. Risk Factors There are no definitive risk factors for long COVID, but some studies suggest associations with: Severe acute COVID-19 illness. A higher number of initial symptoms. Elevated inflammatory markers (e.g., CRP, D-dimer). Decreased lymphocyte counts. Diagnosis The diagnosis of long COVID is primarily clinical, based on the persistence of symptoms for at least two months following acute COVID-19, without an alternative explanation. Symptoms can involve multiple organ systems, and no specific laboratory or imaging findings are diagnostic. Treatment Management of long COVID is multidisciplinary and supportive, focusing on individualized rehabilitation and self-management. Specific treatments include: Dyspnea: Oxygen therapy, breathing exercises (e.g., pursed-lip breathing, deep breathing), and pulmonary rehabilitation. Referral to a cardiologist or pulmonologist may be necessary for underlying cardiac or pulmonary disease. Cough: Managed similarly to post-viral cough syndrome, with attention to contributing factors such as gastroesophageal reflux disease or asthma. Over-the-counter cough suppressants (e.g., benzonatate, guaifenesin, dextromethorphan) may be used. Cardiac injury: Patients with evidence of cardiac injury should be referred to cardiology services. Cardiac rehabilitation may be indicated for those with impaired functional status. Prognosis The natural history and long-term prognosis of long COVID remain incompletely understood. Symptoms may persist, fluctuate, or relapse over time, significantly impacting patients' quality of life and daily functioning. Further research is needed to better understand the condition and develop targeted therapies.
